Random number generation on STM32

To look at the details of random number generation in an embedded environment, I used an STM32 chip to compare four different generators, from C's standard rand() function to an external 24-bit ADC. I rendered the output as RGB565 colour matrices, so the results could be visually inspected.

Random number generation

Entropy and random numbers

Entropy is important for encryption - secret keys need to be difficult to guess or reproduce. Randomness is also useful in games and in communication, where outcomes need to be unexpected, and random delays are used to reduced the likelihood of transmission conflicts.

Pseudorandom generators and physical noise

A pseudorandom generator produces a repeatable sequence from a seed. It does not create fresh entropy. Practical secure systems often combine a physical entropy source with a cryptographically secure generator.

Test setup

Two random generators used software routines. The third test sampled the STM32's internal temperature sensor through its ADC, and used the reading's lower noisy bit to construct a uint16_t. The fourth test used an external 24-bit ADC, and used the lower noisy 4 and 5 bits to construct a uint16_t.

Comparing the output

The generated colour matrix images provided a visual comparison of the four random number generation method. Getting good entropy is a serious matter, especially when cryptographic security relies on it.
